newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy tames inflation, awaits rate reward.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy tames inflation, awaits rate reward.

text.p: Italy's latest set of upbeat inflation figures show it is on the way to taming one of its biggest bug-bears, and economists said on Wednesday the country should not have long to wait to reap an interest rate reward.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who is hoping the Bank of Italy will act soon on rates and lower the interest bill on the government's debt mountain, hailed preliminary consumer price data, saying the economy now appeared to have turned the corner.
Analysts said data from 10 cities out this week, which pointed to an October inflation rate of 3.0 percent, could even encourage the central bank to be a bit more bold in 1997.
It raised rates twice in 1995 and waited 14 months before finally being persuaded to cut its key discount rate in July.

Most analysts now expect to see a cut of at least 75 basis points, if not a whole percentage point, around this time next month. One said the usually cautious Bank might even clip a quick 50 basis points off the 8.25 percent rate on Friday.

"The possibility (of a Friday cut) is slightly less than evens," said Craig Shute, analyst at Bear Stearns International in London. "We've seen good wholesale and producer prices...you just can't rule it out. The backdrop is favourable."
If final October prices data out on November 6 confirm analyst forecasts of 3.0 percent consumer price inflation (CPI) growth, it would be the lowest since the June 1969 rate of 2.5 percent.
The inflation rate was 3.4 percent year-on-year in September and 5.8 percent in October last year. Prices peaked last year at six percent in November.

"Consumer inflation growth has passed from 4.5 percent year-on-year in April to three percent in October with good prospects for a further reduction in the coming months," Prodi, a former economics professor, told a conference in Rome.
He said gross domestic product grew 0.5 percent in the third quarter compared with the second quarter, another good omen.
"This makes one think that the most negative period for the economy is now past," he said.

Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas in London, said the Bank of Italy should soon reward Prodi's centre-left government for a 1997 austerity budget designed to slash a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) off next year's deficit.
"Provided the government does its bit on fiscal policy, the Bank of Italy will do its bit on monetary policy."

He said the CPI data showed Italy was effectively catching up with the low inflation economic climate elsewhere in Europe and the United States. It could augur well for the lira's re-entry into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).
"Provided the central rate (against the mark) is realistic and sustainable, around 1,000-1,025 ... I would argue (the Bank) could cut rates even more," he added.

Analysts said Italy could be heading for a "mega-weekend" in late November when the budget could be passed in the lower house of parliament, the lira could be readmitted to the ERM and the Bank of Italy could cut the discount rate.
"It's quite possible," Wattret said. Successful passage of the budget through the Chamber of Deputies by the scheduled date of November 17 is seen as the trigger for the other two events.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Tuesday that the CPI data pointed to a "culture of stability" taking root.

Giorgio Radaelli, at Lehman Brothers in London, said he expected further swift strides, with November inflation of 2.4 to 2.7 percent. And a Reuter survey of 13 economists forecast the bank would follow up with another rate cut early next year. ($1=1480 Lire)
